The scammer did not ask for money immediately after he succeeded, but continued to observe the conversation. When committing the crime, he pretended to be a company employee, used deepfake technology to imitate his voice, and instructed the victim through voice messages to transfer the virtual assets to another wallet.

Why is this news important?

  • Explain that "sounds like a colleague" may be synthesized audio.
  • High value transfers require dual person/dual channel confirmation beyond chat and voice.
  • When accounts are synced silently (e.g. by linking devices), scammers can gain tone and business context.

HoldLine corresponding reading: AI voice impersonation topic + related equipment manual + business number protection.

12-uk-actionfraud-code.title: UK Action Fraud: Pretending to be a friend and asking for a six-digit activation code, the number of reports is rising
12-uk-actionfraud-code.excerpt: The scammer first takes over the account of an acquaintance, and then asks for the verification code on the grounds that "the verification code was sent incorrectly"; the official suggested THINK. CALL. and two-step verification.
12-uk-actionfraud-code.body:
UK anti-fraud agency Action Fraud has warned that it has received more than 60 reports related to WhatsApp account takeovers. After the scammer takes control of someone's account in your address book, they will first exchange normal greetings, and at the same time use your number to trigger a six-digit activation code text message, and then falsely claim that the code was sent incorrectly and ask you to forward it.

Official recommendations for action

  • Report and block within the app.
  • Never share activation codes.
  • THINK. CALL.——For abnormal requests, call first to confirm.
  • Settings → Account → Two-Step Verification → Turn on.

Although the warning was issued earlier, the attack template it describes is highly homogeneous with the 2024-2026 notifications from Singapore, Ireland, and Switzerland, indicating that this is a "standard operating procedure" that spans multiple years and across countries.

13-uk-actionfraud-groups.title: Community and religious groups become targets: first deceive the registration code, and then ask for emergency help from the group members
13-uk-actionfraud-groups.excerpt: Action Fraud said it had received 268 reports since January of that year; scammers infiltrated large community/religious groups and asked for one-time passwords in the name of video call registration.
13-uk-actionfraud-groups.body:
Another Action Fraud alert focused on large community, alumni, work and religious WhatsApp groups. The scammer may first use a fake avatar/nickname to gain trust, and then ask for a registration code in the name of "joining a group video call requires a one-time password" to move the victim's WhatsApp to a new device. After obtaining it, they can turn on two-step verification to lock the original owner, and ask for an emergency loan from group friends or relatives.

Why group environments are more dangerous

  • Members have a culture of "mutual help" among themselves, and the success rate of emergency help is higher.
  • Nicknames and avatars in the group are easy to imitate.
  • One takeover can reach dozens or hundreds of people.

Administrators should encourage all members to enable two-step verification and stipulate that any request for code or money in the group must be verified off-site.

14-malaysia-mcmc-2026-09.title: MCMC: Pay attention to complaints about WhatsApp being hacked/blocked, and be wary of charging for "recovery services"
14-malaysia-mcmc-2026-09.excerpt: The committee distinguishes between "account takeover" and "platform ban"; it reminds not to share verification codes and PINs, not to trust paid recovery agencies, and to use official channels.
14-malaysia-mcmc-2026-09.body:
On September 25, 2026, MCMC issued a media statement stating that it had noticed public concerns about WhatsApp accounts being hacked, blocked or unusable, and had referred relevant cases to Meta for clarification and processing. The statement specifically clarified: After an account is taken over by an illegal person, it may be spammed with fraudulent/spam messages and violate the terms of service, and then be banned by the platform - these are two related but different problems.

Key reminders for users

  • Reinstate or appeal through WhatsApp official channels.
  • Don't share verification codes or security PINs.
  • Turn on two-step verification and stay away from suspicious links and unknown apps.
  • Be wary of "retrieval" services that require fees, personal information, or verification codes.

HoldLine added: Anyone who asks you to "give the verification code to him before you can retrieve it" may be committing a second fraud.

15-india-call-merge.source: Publicly available technical/police interview reports (such as Indian Express, etc.)
15-india-call-merge.title: India Observation: OTP phishing, SIM card replacement, combined call code listening and multi-line parallelization
15-india-call-merge.excerpt: The report combed through how scammers combined social engineering and telecommunications methods to take over WhatsApp, and quoted Meta’s recommendations: never share six-digit codes and enable two-step verification.
15-india-call-merge.body:
Mainstream technology reports in India summarize various takeover paths: OTP phishing (fake customer service/fake friends ask for codes), SIM swapping (receiving text messages after the number card is transferred), short physical contact and then association with WhatsApp Web, and "merged calls" that allow the victim to connect to the verification voice and listen to the OTP without knowing it.

Red flags worth remembering

  • Received a WhatsApp verification code without requesting it.
  • My friend suddenly wants OTP.
  • Logged out for no reason.
  • Prompt number to register on new device.

Protection combination

The report and Meta's response jointly emphasized: do not share PIN/verification code, enable two-step verification, carefully combine unknown calls, regularly check associated devices, and limit the scope of privacy visibility. For Chinese readers, these entries correspond one-to-one with HoldLine 01–08 and 17.

16-eset-linked-devices.source: ESET and other security research articles
16-eset-linked-devices.title: Security manufacturer reminds: Associated devices are synchronized silently, and the phone “looks normal” has also been exposed
16-eset-linked-devices.excerpt: The quickest self-check is to open "Connected Devices"; unfamiliar browser sessions should be logged out immediately. And emphasize that the two-step verification must be bound to the recovery email address.
16-eset-linked-devices.body:
Security articles such as ESET point out that many users think that "if they are not kicked offline, they are not stolen." An attacker could actually just hang onto a WhatsApp web/desktop session and read the chat in real time. 30-second self-test method: Settings → Linked Devices, log out if you don’t recognize it.

Other signs of compromise

  • You have to log in again after logging out abnormally.
  • A reply to your unsent message appears.
  • Contact feedback is abnormal.

Importance of recovering your mailbox

The article emphasizes that you must add a recovery email when two-step verification is turned on - if someone else sets a PIN first, the presence of an email may determine whether you can retrieve it in a few minutes or wait for many days. This is consistent with recapture instructions from the WhatsApp Help Center.

17-scamshield-explain.title: ScamShield Illustration: Four Steps to WhatsApp Takeover, and Why “Anyone Asking for OTP is a Scam”
17-scamshield-explain.excerpt: The official Q&A breaks down the attack into four steps: triggering OTP, asking for codes from acquaintances, kicking people offline, and spreading impersonation. It also provides two-step verification and related device cleaning guidelines.
17-scamshield-explain.body:
The Q&A related to ScamShield in Singapore describes the takeover in a very clear four-step manner: 1) The scammer logs in with your account to trigger the OTP; 2) The stolen contacts come and ask you to forward them; 3) You are logged out after handing them over; 4) The scammer uses your identity to repeatedly deceive others.

Official primary level reminder

Any request to share a WhatsApp OTP, no matter who it appears to be from, should be considered a scam. OTP belongs only to the recipient; neither the platform nor the "customer service" will ask for codes like this.

protection list

  • Never share OTP
  • Turn on two-step verification
  • Review and remove unfamiliar associated devices
  • If stolen, notify contacts using non-WhatsApp channels

18-whatsapp-official-security.title: WhatsApp official safe page: 2-step verification, only authentic ones, group control and reporting tools
18-whatsapp-official-security.excerpt: The platform reiterates its multi-layered protection and user-operable switches; it is clear that counterfeit clients will bring serious privacy and security risks.
18-whatsapp-official-security.body:
WhatsApp's official security center outlines its default privacy, spam detection, abnormal takeover prompts and other capabilities, and gives users a list of things to do: turn on two-step verification, always use official apps, manage groups and add permissions, learn to identify scams, make good use of blocking and reporting, and re-register to regain the account when necessary.

What it means to readers of "Download Software Anti-Theft"

The official position is very clear: use the genuine client and built-in switch first, rather than looking for third-party "anti-theft plug-ins" of unknown origin. The sorting of the HoldLine tool page also follows this principle.

The value of reporting

Reporting does not necessarily allow you to immediately recover your losses, but it can help the platform crack down on abusive accounts and reduce the probability that your address book will continue to be targeted accurately.

19-jamaica-cirt.title: Jamaica CIRT: Phishing and hijacking coexist, it is emphasized to log out of the associated device and re-enable two-step verification
19-jamaica-cirt.excerpt: The alert describes the risk of malicious links and account hijacking; if you suspect it has been compromised, you should clean the associated device, reset the two-step verification, and report phishing to spam@whatsapp.com and other channels (subject to the current official guidelines).
19-jamaica-cirt.body:
Jamaica's Cyber ​​Security Incident Response Team has issued a rising threat alert for WhatsApp users, noting that scam messages go hand in hand with account hijacking. Phishing may disguise itself as a formal organization and induce people to click on a fake login page or hand over a verification code; after a successful hijack, they can impersonate the victim, read contacts and spread.

Technical actions after the fall (summary of reports)

  • Settings → Linked Devices: Log out all unknown devices.
  • Re-enable/reset two-step verification.
  • Alert contacts.
  • Report fishing samples according to official instructions.

This alert is once again aligned with the European, American and Asian press releases: Cleaning associated devices + two-step verification is an international first aid kit.

20-meta-scam-accounts-takedown.title: Platform Governance Profile: Meta reveals WhatsApp account of the Center to Combat Fraudulent Advertising and Related Scams
20-meta-scam-accounts-takedown.excerpt: The report quoted: Meta will cancel more than 6.8 million WhatsApp accounts related to fraud centers in the first half of 2025; at the same time, users are reminded that they still need to protect themselves.
20-meta-scam-accounts-takedown.body:
In public statements on technology crimes held in Hong Kong and other regions, reports cited Meta data: In the first half of 2025, more than 6.8 million WhatsApp accounts related to fraud centers were revoked, and a large number of fraudulent advertisements were cleared on other platforms. This shows that the platform side is continuing to crack down, but it cannot replace the two-step verification and verification code discipline on the user side.

The correct way to read this article

  • Don’t relax your personal settings just because “the platform will ban your account”.
  • Accounts that are stolen and used for mass messaging may be blocked quickly, but your relatives and friends may have completed the transfer before being blocked.
  • The fastest action I can take is still: don’t give me the code, open a two-step process, clear the equipment, and verify before asking for money.

The conclusion of the international news collection: from the Caribbean to Western Europe, from Southeast Asia to East Asia, the details of the discourse are different, but the structure is highly similar. Think of HoldLine's 30 long articles as an "operation manual" and this page as a wall of evidence for "why you need to do it now."

newsIntro.title: International news: Latest observations on WhatsApp theft and account takeover
newsIntro.lead: The following 20 articles are feature articles compiled by HoldLine based on police, network security agencies and public reports from various countries, focusing on recent trends such as WhatsApp account takeovers, code fraud, fake voting and fake borrowing. The data and dates in this article are from the public release; the interface and loss figures may be adjusted according to subsequent statistics, please refer to the original organization's release.

toolsIntro.title: Recommended downloads: Software and tools to reduce the risk of WhatsApp theft
toolsIntro.lead: There is no "one-click anti-theft artifact". What is really effective is: official WhatsApp, system security capabilities, formal anti-fraud apps, plus two-step verification and verification code discipline. This page only recommends tools that can be obtained from official channels, and clearly states what it can and cannot do.

whatsapp-official.name: WhatsApp official client
whatsapp-official.summary: The only instant messaging body that should be installed. Modified versions, enhanced versions, and network disk APKs are all high-risk.
why: Only official clients will continue to receive security updates, fraud tips, and account recovery capabilities.
Unofficial packages may have built-in backdoors, and end-to-end encryption cannot save "the endpoint has been compromised."
The police and Meta have repeatedly reminded: Only use WhatsApp from the official app store.
steps: iPhone: Search WhatsApp Messenger installation/update from App Store only.
Android: Priority is given to Google Play; in some regions, the official version in the official app store of the mobile phone manufacturer is available.
Immediately after installation, turn on two-step verification and check "Linked Devices".
whatsapp-official.stepsCaption: Install from the official store and turn on two-step verification immediately
whatsapp-official.caution: Do not download the so-called Plus/GB/Anti-withdrawal version from group files, network disks, or short links.

whatsapp-desktop.name: WhatsApp Desktop/Web (Official)
whatsapp-desktop.summary: It is convenient for computer to reply, but it must be connected from the official entrance; log out on the mobile phone immediately after using the public computer.
why: The official desktop version is much safer than the casually searched "Web login page".
Associated devices are common entry points for silent peeping, and regular clients allow you to proactively manage sessions.
steps: On mobile WhatsApp → Linked devices → Link new device.
Open the official desktop application on your computer, or manually enter the official webpage address in your browser and scan the QR code.
Do not check Keep logged in when using public devices; return to your mobile phone to kick off the session after use.
whatsapp-desktop.stepsCaption: Device associated with mobile phone → official scan code → log out after use
whatsapp-desktop.caution: Never scan the "Login/Vote" QR code displayed in chat or on an unfamiliar website.

builtin-security.name: WhatsApp built-in security (free)
builtin-security.summary: Two-step verification, Scam Alert, app lock, privacy restrictions - no need to install a third-party "anti-theft plug-in".
why: Two-step verification directly increases the cost of taking over, which is a standard recommendation in police drafts in various countries.
Scam Alert can prompt suspicious sessions on the device side (depending on whether your version provides it).
App Lock reduces the risk of "the phone being unlocked and being opened easily".
steps: Settings → Account → Two-step verification → Enable and bind a login email address.
Find Scam Alert (if available) in settings and turn it on.
Turn on application lock (fingerprint/face); restrict strangers from joining groups in privacy.
Check "Linked Devices" once a week.
builtin-security.stepsCaption: Set up two-step verification for your account and bind your recovery email
builtin-security.caution: Built-in functionality doesn’t stop you from proactively sending verification codes to scammers—discipline is still the first line of defense.

links.label: How to protect against suspicious messages (Help Center)

scamshield.name: ScamShield (Singapore Anti-Fraud Suite)
scamshield.summary: Singapore government-related anti-fraud tools: can help intercept suspicious calls/text messages and check suspicious messages. Local users strongly recommend installation.
why: When the Singapore police report cases of WhatsApp account theft and fake money lending, they often directly recommend installing ScamShield.
It can filter some fraudulent text messages and calls and reduce the arrival rate of "fraud phone calls/phishing text messages".
The official website provides verification channels and early warning information.
steps: Only install from official short links or App Store / Google Play.
Follow the instructions to enable call/text message filtering related permissions.
If you encounter a suspicious request, you can verify it by combining its verification function and hotline channels.
scamshield.stepsCaption: Download from the official store and enable filtering permissions
scamshield.caution: It may not be applicable to non-Singapore numbers/environments; do not download fake "ScamShield" copycat packages.

scameter.name: Scameter / Scameter+ (Hong Kong anti-fraud video app)
scameter.summary: The fraud detection tool promoted by the Hong Kong police can be used to verify suspicious platforms, accounts, etc. Hong Kong users are recommended to use it together.
why: WhatsApp accounts for a very high proportion of "online account hijacking" cases in Hong Kong, and the police continue to call for the use of official anti-fraud tools.
Verification before transferring money or clicking can reduce secondary financial losses after account theft.
steps: Enter Scameter through Hong Kong Police CyberDefender / official announcement channels.
Check unfamiliar payment accounts and suspicious websites before proceeding.
At the same time, enable two-step verification on WhatsApp and inventory associated devices.
scameter.stepsCaption: Official portal to verify suspicious links or accounts
scameter.caution: Verification tools cannot replace "not giving a verification code"; account hacking itself still depends on account settings and habits.

links.label: Hong Kong government related anti-fraud information portal

play-protect.name: Google Play Protection Mechanism/System Security Update
play-protect.summary: Let the system and app store block a large number of malicious installation packages for you, reducing the risk of Trojans stealing text messages and screens.
why: Some stolen accounts will cooperate with malicious apps to read notifications or assist in operations.
Timely system patches can narrow the window of known vulnerabilities.
steps: Android: Turn on Google Play Protect; only allow installation from official stores.
iOS/Android: Turn on automatic updates and install system patches regularly.
Refuse the temporary temptation to allow installation from unknown sources.
play-protect.stepsCaption: Turn on system protection and keep it updated
play-protect.caution: System protection cannot stop social engineering deception; it is the equipment layer, not the language layer.

password-manager.name: Password manager (safeguards 2-step verification PINs)
password-manager.summary: Used to safely store WhatsApp two-step verification PIN and email password to avoid setting weak passwords or writing them in chats.
why: Many people set up 123456 for fear of forgetting, or send their PIN to another chat backup - which is even more dangerous.
A legitimate password manager can generate and encrypt strong passwords.
steps: Install trusted products such as Bitwarden, 1Password, or the system's own keychain/password from the official store.
Create a separate record for WhatsApp 2-step verification PIN.
The password manager itself turns on strong master passwords and biometrics.
password-manager.stepsCaption: Safely store PINs with a password vault
password-manager.caution: Do not use unknown "PIN to save the App"; do not save the PIN in the unencrypted memo cloud and synchronize it everywhere.

mobile-antivirus.name: Regular mobile phone security software (anti-Trojan, not anti-fraud)
mobile-antivirus.summary: If you often sideload applications or the device environment is complex, you can choose a security suite from a well-known manufacturer; it mainly protects against malware, not against acquaintances.
why: Can assist in discovering suspicious applications and phishing sites (capabilities vary by product).
It has certain value against threats such as "SMS Stealing Trojans".
steps: Only install well-known products from Google Play / App Store (like Malwarebytes, Bitdefender, etc., select as per availability in your region).
After installation, do a full scan and review applications with abnormal SMS/accessibility permissions.
Don't stack multiple conflicting security suites at the same time.
mobile-antivirus.stepsCaption: Scan the entire disk after installation in the official store
mobile-antivirus.caution: No anti-virus can prevent you from handing over the verification code; nor can you download the nameless APK of "WhatsApp Killer and Stealer".
